39, ending 27 September 2026 7 October 2026 | Emergency situation update Download (5.8 MB) Overview In week 39 2026, globally, influenza positivity was below 10% and SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low. Influenza positivity was below 10% in the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas and at 10% in the tropical areas. Influenza positivity was below 10% in the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas with a decrease in the reported specimens tested in the most recent week. RSV positivity also remained low globally. Influenza Globally, influenza detections remained low in week 39 with influenza A virus detections predominant. An increase in the proportion of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 detections has been observed over recent weeks. In the southern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in single countries in Tropical and Temperate South America and Eastern Africa. Percent positivity was over 30% in single countries in South-East Asia and Oceania. Increases in activity were reported in single countries in Temperate South America and South-East Asia. In the northern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in some countries in Western Africa, Southern, South-East and Eastern Asia and in a single country in Central America and the Caribbean and Western Asia. Percent positivity was over 30% in some countries in Western, Southern and South-East Asia and in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Western Africa. Increases in activity were observed in some countries in Western and South-East Asia and in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Western Africa and Southern Asia. In the zones with elevated positivity, influenza A(H3N2) was predominant in Eastern Asia; influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 was predominant in Western, Southern and South-East Asia and influenza B was predominant in Tropical and Temperate South America. Influenza A and B were codominant in Central America and the Caribbean and Western Africa and influenza A(H3N2) and influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 were codominant in Oceania. SARS-CoV-2 Globally, SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low across most reporting countries, with elevated positivity (>10%) reported in some countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Eastern Asia, and in single countries in South West and Northern Europe and South-East Asia. A medium increase in activity was observed in a single country in Central America and the Caribbean, and small increases in activity were observed in single countries in South West and Eastern Europe. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) RSV positivity was elevated (>10%) in a few countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Temperate South America and in a single country in Tropical South America. Percent positivity was over 30% in a single country in Southern Asia. A small increase in activity was observed in a single country in Central America and the Caribbean. RSV and influenza activity were both elevated in countries in Temperate South America and Southern Asia. Severity assessment The severity assessments here are reported from countries, areas and territories. Assessments for transmissibility can be reported based on syndromic parameters and/or influenza-specific parameters. In the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country and low in a single country; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country. In the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in 13 countries, low in a single country and moderate in a single country; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in eight countries and low in a single country. Influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country in the tropical areas. WHO encourages countries, especially those that have received the multiplex influenza and SARS-CoV-2 reagent kits from GISRS, to conduct integrated surveillance of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 and report epidemiological and laboratory information in a timely manner to established regional and global platforms. The guidance can be found here. Starting with report #501, the Global Respiratory Virus Activity Weekly Update included data from sentinel surveillance and other types of systematically conducted virologic surveillance. Countries, areas, and territories use a variety of approaches to monitor respiratory virus activity and data in this report may vary from surveillance reports posted elsewhere. Analyses stratified by source of surveillance is available through Respimart. records.content: https://ukhsa.blog.gov.uk/2026/10/08/are-we-seeing-an-early-flu-season-what-we-know-so-far-about-this-years-strains/ Early signs suggest that flu season may be starting earlier this year. According to our winter virus surveillance data , flu activity throughout September has been higher than in the same period over the past 4 winters. While levels remain at baseline, meaning still relatively low overall, the upward trend - if it continues in the coming weeks - suggests an early flu season. The rise so far has been driven largely by cases in the 18- to 24-year-old age group. What strains are circulating this year? So far this season, there's a mix of 2 flu A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2, circulating in England. The flu vaccine is designed to protect against all 3 main types of flu: influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and influenza B. Whichever ends up dominating this winter - or if they all circulate at similar levels throughout - the vaccine should offer broad protection. It might help to think of the flu vaccine like packing for a winter trip: you bring layers for rain, snow and wind because you don't know exactly what the weather will throw at you. The vaccine works the same way, offering layered protection against all 3 flu types so you're prepared, whatever ends up circulating. What is a 'drifted' strain? Flu viruses are constantly changing through a natural process called antigenic drift. Each year, the World Health Organization monitors circulating strains globally and selects which ones should be targeted by that season's vaccine, but this decision has to be made months in advance, to give manufacturers time to produce enough doses. Sometimes the virus continues to change after that point, resulting in it no longer matching the vaccine strain as closely as originally predicted. This year, it's the A(H1N1) subtype that has drifted from the strain used in the vaccine . It's still too early in the season to know for certain whether this drifted H1N1 will circulate widely in the UK, or how it will affect vaccine effectiveness. How does this compare to last winter? Last winter, a drifted strain of H3N2, known as subclade K, emerged after the vaccine composition for the Northern Hemisphere had already been finalised. Despite this, the vaccine was effective and even with an earlier start to the flu season, overall levels of activity and mortality were lower than the previous year. Modelling suggests the vaccination programme in England prevented around 100,000 hospital admissions and 7,000 deaths that winter. Does the vaccine still work against drifted strains? Drift is a normal and expected part of how flu viruses behave, and experience shows that vaccines typically remain effective at preventing severe illness even when the circulating strain doesn't perfectly match the one used to make the vaccine. Our analysis from last season found vaccinated children were around 65 to 70% less likely to attend or be admitted to hospital with flu, while vaccinated adults were around 20 to 30% less likely. Does this affect when I should get vaccinated? Because flu activity is already trending higher than usual for this point in the year, and because it takes a couple of weeks for the vaccine to provide full protection, getting vaccinated sooner rather than later gives you the best chance of being protected before flu takes hold more widely. If this does turn into an early season, waiting could mean you're exposed during the period before your immunity has had time to build. What's UKHSA doing to keep track of this? UKHSA is continuing to monitor the drifted H1N1 strain through laboratory analysis, routine surveillance of flu's impact on health, and ongoing studies into how well the vaccine is working in practice. This monitoring will continue throughout winter, including watching for any other strains that start to become more prominent. What should I do now? If you're eligible for a free flu vaccine , the advice is simple: don't wait. You can check your eligibility and book an appointment through the NHS App, online, or by contacting your GP practice or a local pharmacy. For school-aged children, most vaccines are delivered in schools by local immunisation teams. Look out for consent forms and return them. Community clinics are available for children who miss school sessions. From 1 December 2026, school-aged children from Reception to Year 11 who did not get vaccinated in school can also get vaccinated at a pharmacy . Given the early signs this season, getting protected now, rather than later, is the best way to guard against serious illness this winter. Tags: flu , H1N1 , H3N2 , influenza , vaccination

Over the past week, the incidence of ARVI has decreased by 10.2%. According to epidemiological monitoring data, three cases of influenza were registered in the capital, Astana, and two in the Mangistau region. A total of 834 samples were analyzed as part of the study, of which five tested positive. In the past week, the country recorded 127,266 cases of ARVI, which is 13,007 fewer compared to the previous week when 140,273 cases were registered. Since the beginning of September, the total number of cases has reached 760,182. Additionally, 68 cases of rhinovirus infection, 47 cases of coronavirus infections, 50 cases of bocavirus infection, 32 cases of parainfluenza, 27 cases of adenovirus infection, two cases of respiratory syncytial infection, and one case of metapneumovirus infection have been identified in Kazakhstan. The Ministry of Health also emphasized that 2.1 million doses of the "Grippol Plus" vaccine have been purchased for free vaccination of the population against influenza. The vaccine is available in all regions of the country, and as of October 7, 240,375 people have been vaccinated. Iowa State University October 9, 2026 schedule4 Min Read National Pork Board By Michael Zeller, Hu Ke, Phillip Gauger, Quyen Le, Daniel Linhares and Giovani Trevisan, Iowa State University A snapshot of swine influenza A virus activity in 2026 SDRS influenza A virus RT-rtPCR surveillance detection data through August 2026 showed contrasting patterns between production phases. IAV positivity in adult/sow farm submissions declined throughout 2026, reaching approximately 10% in August (Figure 1), the lowest level observed since 2014. In contrast, positivity in wean-to-market submissions remained elevated, generally ranging from 30% to 45% during the year, indicating continued IAV circulation among growing pig populations. Figure 1. IAV positivity trends by production phase (Adult/Sow Farm vs Wean-to-Market). To better understand the contribution of IAV to respiratory cases during this period, confirmed tissue diagnoses were further evaluated (Figure 2). Cases involving IAV and at least one additional respiratory pathogen (co-diagnosis) accounted for approximately 13% to 23% of all respiratory tissue diagnoses from January through August 2026, whereas IAV-only cases represented approximately 2% to 5%. The highest number of co-diagnosis cases was observed in February (171 cases; 22% of respiratory diagnoses). Among IAV co-diagnosis cases, the most frequently identified pathogens were PRRSV (37.1%), Streptococcus suis (20.2%), Glaesserella parasuis (14%), and Pasteurella multocida (10.6%), collectively accounting for more than 80% of all co-diagnosis events. In comparison, IAV-only diagnoses remained relatively infrequent throughout the period, ranging from 7 to 31 cases per month and contributing less than 5% of respiratory tissue diagnoses in any month evaluated. Related:Surveillance, vaccines vital to curb African swine fever spread Figure 2. Monthly number and proportion of confirmed respiratory tissue diagnoses in which IAV was identified alone or in combination with at least one additional respiratory pathogen, January-August 2026. Further insight into circulating IAV strains was obtained through subtype detections by participating laboratories (Figure 3). Among 2,005 subtype detections by RT-rtPCR reported from January to August 2026, partially characterized viruses accounted for 613 detections (30.6%), followed by H1N2 with 516 detections (25.7%), H3N2 with 395 detections (19.7%) and H1N1 with 381 detections (19%). Mixed subtype detections represented 87 cases (4.3%), whereas H3N1 was detected infrequently, with 13 detections (0.6%). Overall, H1N1, H1N2 and H3N2 accounted for approximately 64% of all subtype detections reported during 2026. Figure 3. Monthly IAV subtype detection by PCR. These findings provide a current snapshot of IAV activity, disease association and subtype diversity within U.S. swine populations. The following section highlights recent observations and perspectives related to IAV beyond swine surveillance. Changes in H3 diversity in swine influenza H3N2 has been a predominant subtype in North American swine influenza ecology since the late 1990s, accounting for 20%-33% of the annual influenza detections between 2007 to 2026. During this time, the composition of the genetic clades has shifted substantially. In the decade prior to 2026, approximately 40% of the H3N2 cases belonged to clade 3.1990.4a (formerly Cluster IVA), while another 40% to clade 3.2010.1 (formerly 2010.1). Most of the remaining detections were other 3.1990.4 clades, primarily 3.1990.4b (formerly cluster IVB). By 2025, clade 3.2010.1 accounted for approximately 70% of all H3 detections and increased further to over 85% in August, 2026. In contrast, detections of 3.1990.4a declined to just 4% in 2025. There has been a notable increase of detections of 3.1990.4i, which rose to nearly 6% in 2025. Another notable trend since 2023 has been the growing number of H3 viruses introduced into swine through human-to-swine transmission, referred to as spillover events. Related:SDSU Swine Day highlights student research, industry insights Between November 2022 and August 2026, 77 introductions of human-origin H3 viruses were detected in the U.S. swine population. In many cases, these viruses are genetically similar to H3 strains that were circulating in humans at the time of the spillover event. The human-derived clades detected in swine include G.1.1, G.2, G.2.2, J.2, J.2.5, and K. These spillover viruses can be readily monitored because they do not share a recent common ancestor with contemporary swine H3 viruses. To track these human-derived H3 in pigs, a phylogenetic based investigation using both swine and contemporary human H3 to understand how these viruses evolve after entering the swine population. This approach has shown that while many detections appear to represent recent spillover events, some G.1.1 viruses continue to circulate within swine populations and now form a distinct evolutionary group, suggesting ongoing swine-to-swine transmission and the establishment of a new H3 genetic clade. Related:United Animal Health names Brian Barker president and CEO Previous spillover H3 viruses, such as 3.2010.1 and 3.2010.2, underwent reassortment before becoming widely established in swine. Although reassortment may not be required for a spillover virus to become endemic, it appears to improve the likelihood of successful adaptation and spread among pigs. The G.1.1 viruses detected recently in swine have also undergone reassortment. Detections from 2025 onwards contain a human-origin G.1.1 H3 paired with a swine-origin N2.2002B neuraminidase. The remaining internal genes consist of a triple-reassortant polymerase complex and non-structural segment, along with pandemic-origin matrix and nucleoprotein segments. Viruses with this genetic configuration have been detected in Illinois, Iowa and Minnesota. Whether this lineage will continue to spread and become established across North American swine populations remains unknown. However, its emergence highlights the ongoing role of human-to-swine transmission in generating new genetic diversity within the H3 influenza population. Sign In Follow US Health Greece launches seasonal influenza vaccination campaign with 3.64 million doses Greece: New flu vaccines in 2026 Last updated: 11/10/2026 1:05 pm Ali Ragab ByAli Ragab News Editor Ali Ragab, editor at Voice of Emirates News Agency, Cairo office, is an Egyptian journalist and poet, a member of the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate, specializing in... - News Editor 2 days ago Share 4 Min Read Flu vaccination campaign in Greece (Photo/Archive) SHARE Summarize with AI Summarize Summarize with AI ChatGPT Claude Perplexity Grok Copy Prompt Highlights Nasal vaccine for children and groups subject to the warning Optimal Timing and Vaccination Priorities Athens, Greece – Greek health authorities have announced the launch of the seasonal influenza vaccination campaign for the new year. Since the vaccination period began on October 2, 30% of the allocated vaccines have been distributed to pharmacies across the country. Total imported shipments for the year are expected to reach approximately 3.64 million doses, compared to 3.5 million doses during the previous season. This initiative is part of a comprehensive plan to curb the spread of the seasonal virus and protect groups most at risk of complications. Manolis Katsarakis, Secretary-General of the Panhellenic Pharmaceutical Association (PFS), confirmed the availability of sufficient and diverse vaccine supplies to meet national needs. He noted a significant, steady rise in influenza vaccination rates in recent years: approximately 1.4 million doses were administered via pharmacies during the 2023–2024 season, rising to 1.92 million in 2024–2025, and reaching 2.04 million in 2025–2026. The official explained that around 460,000 doses of enhanced vaccines—which provide a stronger immune response in the elderly and individuals with organ failure—had been imported. However, if the enhanced vaccine is unavailable for those over the age of 65, the recommendation is to proceed with vaccination using any available conventional vaccine rather than delaying immunization. Nasal vaccine for children and groups subject to the warning For the second consecutive year, the live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) has been made available in an increased quantity of 200,000 doses. Administered under the supervision of pediatricians, it comes as a nasal spray intended for children and adolescents aged 2 to 18. Health authorities have warned against administering the nasal vaccine to children suffering from bronchial asthma or those who have experienced recurrent wheezing episodes within the past 12 months. Administration is also contraindicated for children with immunodeficiency or those undergoing long-term aspirin therapy; in such cases, the use of the traditional inactivated injectable vaccine is recommended. Furthermore, close contact with severely immunocompromised individuals must be avoided for seven days following the administration of the live vaccine. Optimal Timing and Vaccination Priorities The period from mid-October to the end of November is the ideal time for vaccination, as the body requires approximately two weeks to develop the necessary immunity before peak influenza activity in Greece. This peak typically begins in January and reaches its height during February and March. High-priority groups for vaccination include individuals over the age of 60, infants and children aged six months to five years, pregnant women, and those with chronic conditions (such as diabetes, neuromuscular disorders, and morbid obesity). Medical personnel and staff at elderly care facilities are also included in the priority categories. Most groups require a single annual dose, with the exception of children under the age of nine receiving the vaccine for the first time; they require two doses, spaced at least 28 days apart, to ensure full protection. records.content: Search Site search Kaz Rus Eng KazTAG Astana, 6:51 | 13 october Kazakh Telegraph Agency Open menu Back Homepage Newsline News of the day Video Categoriesоткрыть меню Standpoint Interview Expert-opinion Replika Photoreports About us Main page — Newsline —Circulation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 strain confirmed in Kazakhstan Circulation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 strain confirmed in Kazakhstan October 12, 2026, 11:13 Astana. October 12. KazTAG – The circulation of the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 strain has been confirmed in Kazakhstan. “The first five cases of seasonal influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 have been registered in Kazakhstan. At the same time, the overall incidence of acute respiratory viral infections (ARVI) fell by 10.2% over the past week. Since the start of the vaccination campaign, more than 240,000 people have received flu shots. According to epidemiological monitoring, three influenza cases were detected in Astana and two in Mangystau Region. A total of 834 laboratory samples were tested, five of which returned positive results,” the press service of the Ministry of Healthcare reported. During the latest reporting week, 127,266 ARVI cases were recorded nationwide, compared with 140,273 the previous week. Since the beginning of September, the cumulative number of ARVI cases has reached 760,182. “Laboratory monitoring also confirms the circulation of other respiratory viruses. Confirmed cases include 68 rhinovirus infections, 47 seasonal coronavirus infections, 50 bocavirus infections, 32 parainfluenza cases, 27 adenovirus infections, two respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) cases and one human metapneumovirus case,” the ministry said. The ministry added that 2.1 million doses of the Grippol Plus vaccine had been procured for free vaccination. “Its composition complies with World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for the 2026–2027 epidemic season. Vaccines have been distributed to all regions. As of October 7, a total of 240,375 people had been vaccinated. Priority for free vaccination is given to high-risk groups, including healthcare workers, pregnant women, children registered for chronic illnesses, orphans, residents and staff of medical and social care facilities, as well as other groups based on epidemiological indications,” the statement reads. The Ministry of Healthcare reminded the public that October is an optimal time for vaccination, as it takes approximately two weeks for protective immunity to develop. records.content: Just In Pakistan Opinion World Business Sports Tech Life & Style Health Today's Paper Magazines TNS Instep Money Matters YOU US Tuesday October 13, 2026 Today's Paper Prayer Timing Epaper Home Just In Pakistan Opinion World Business Sports Tech Life & Style Health Magazines Instep Money Matters YOU US TNS Time to get vaccinated against flu, influenza A virus Islamabad By Muhammad Qasim October 08, 2026 Representational image of vaccination. — Unsplash/File Islamabad:It is time for the community particularly the high-risk population including chronic patients and those who are immuno-compromised to get vaccinated against flu strains and influenza A disease that appears in winter every year posing serious health threats to the public. Health experts believe that it is need of the time to create awareness among the public about protection against influenza A virus. Prevention from influenza A virus is the best option and people must opt for getting themselves vaccinated against the infection. It is important that the vaccine made available in the market against influenza A is developed from strains of viruses circulating in the world in the previous year and the new vaccine is launched in the market in October every year. Health care providers, children under five, pregnant women, elderly and those having co-morbid conditions including heart or kidney disease or those who are immuno-compromised including patients suffering from diabetes are considered as high-risk population as they are most at risk of contracting seasonal ‘influenza A’ disease. The experts say that influenza A virus may start hitting population in the coming days and it is the best option for at least the most vulnerable population to get vaccinated against flu before the advent of winter. Studies reveal that the flu vaccine made available in the market gives protection for one year against seasonal flu containing virus developed by mutation of DNA of Human, Avian and Swine influenza viruses. The disease season starts in winter. It is worth mentioning here that the disease, now called as seasonal flu, has causes considerable morbidity and mortality in the previous years in the winter months. It is the same disease that had affected thousands of people globally and was named as Inluenza A H1 N1 2009 infection and the same virus has somehow or the other become less virulent with mutation of virus and addition of other strains and is now known as Seasonal Flu, the world over. They say that the concerned health authorities must direct all public sector hospitals to work out a high level of preparedness to deal with the patients of seasonal flu in the high transmission season by developing standard isolation units, stockpiling of PPEs (personal protective equipment), capacity building in the art of infection control and adopting barrier nursing techniques along with procuring sufficient viral transport media and reagents for laboratories. A new epidemiological study from Jiande, a county-level city within Hangzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang Province, offers a detailed look at how laboratory-confirmed influenza A and B cases behave over time and, more importantly, how their future trajectories might be forecast with greater precision. The research, published in BMC Infectious Diseases by Fenglong Zhu and Guisheng Liu of the First People’s Hospital of Jiande together with Cong Huang of Panzhihua Central Hospital, describes a hybrid statistical and machine-learning approach that combines two very different modelling traditions into a single forecasting engine. The study rests on a deceptively simple foundation: six years of hospital-based surveillance data. The researchers extracted records of laboratory-confirmed positive influenza A and B cases spanning January 2019 through December 2024 from the medical-record registration system at the Jiande Branch of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Because the data were drawn from routine diagnostic testing rather than sentinel sampling or syndromic estimates, they represent a direct count of virologically confirmed infections presenting to a single healthcare institution. That characteristic gives the series a certain fidelity, though it also means the counts reflect the population that sought care and tested positive at that hospital rather than the true incidence of influenza in the wider community. Discover more Read Horoscopes Donate to Research Track Outbreaks Before any forecasting could begin, the team characterised the epidemiological rhythm embedded in the data. The analysis revealed distinct seasonal patterns for both influenza types, with epidemic peaks occurring predominantly in winter and spring. This seasonality is the classic signature of influenza in temperate and subtropical regions, driven by a combination of factors including humidity and temperature, human behaviour that concentrates people indoors during colder months, and the survival characteristics of the virus itself in aerosols and on surfaces. Knowing that the seasonal wave will come is one thing; knowing how large it will be and when exactly it will crest is quite another, and that is precisely the gap the authors set out to narrow. Discover more Get Cold Relief Check Forecasts Track Weather Read Ghost Books The first half of the hybrid model is the seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average model, or SARIMA, a workhorse of classical time-series analysis. SARIMA models describe a series as a function of its own past values, past forecast errors, and seasonal counterparts of both, after differencing the data to achieve stationarity. In this study, the model structure was selected systematically: the authors examined autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation functions and applied formal stationarity tests including the Augmented Dickey-Fuller and Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin procedures, with model adequacy judged by information criteria such as the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. The search converged on a SARIMA(1, 0, 1)(2, 1, 1) with a seasonal period of four for influenza A, and a SARIMA(3, 0, 0)(2, 1, 1) with the same seasonal period for influenza B. The quarterly seasonal differencing captured the annual epidemic cycle compressed into the monthly series, while the autoregressive and moving-average terms handled short-term dependencies within and between seasons. SARIMA models excel at capturing regular, repeating structure, but they are fundamentally linear: they assume that future values relate to past values through fixed linear coefficients. Real epidemic curves are rarely so well behaved. Transmission intensity shifts as susceptible populations deplete, as schools open and close, and as viral evolution produces antigenic drift. The second half of the hybrid, the long short-term memory network, addresses this limitation. LSTM is a form of recurrent neural network designed to learn long-range dependencies in sequential data through gated memory cells that decide what information to retain, update, or discard at each time step. Where SARIMA imposes a rigid mathematical structure, LSTM learns flexible, potentially nonlinear mappings from past observations to future values, making it well suited to the irregularities that a seasonal statistical model smooths over. Discover more Health health Get Health Tips The hybrid SARIMA-LSTM architecture used here follows a logic of decomposition and residual learning. The SARIMA component first models the predictable seasonal and linear structure of the case-count series. What remains after SARIMA has done its work, the residual component, contains the nonlinear and irregular dynamics that the classical model cannot express. The LSTM is then trained on this residual signal, learning to correct the SARIMA forecast rather than to reproduce the entire series from scratch. The two components are finally recombined so that the seasonal backbone supplied by SARIMA is refined by the neural network’s learned corrections. The full model was implemented in MATLAB R2024a, and the authors have made core code snippets available as supplementary material, a small but meaningful contribution to reproducibility in a field where methodological details are often opaque. To judge whether the added complexity was worthwhile, the researchers held out the 2024 data as an out-of-sample test set, allowing each model to forecast a full year it had never seen. Performance was measured with two standard error metrics: mean absolute error, which captures the average magnitude of forecast mistakes, and root mean square error, which penalises large errors more heavily. The results were consistent across both influenza types. For influenza A, the hybrid model reduced mean absolute error by 7.3 percent and root mean square error by 7.1 percent relative to standalone SARIMA, and achieved a 9.4 percent reduction in mean absolute error and a 4.6 percent reduction in root mean square error relative to standalone LSTM. For influenza B, the improvements were similar or larger: a 7.5 percent reduction in both error metrics compared with SARIMA, and reductions of 8.9 percent in mean absolute error and 9.5 percent in root mean square error compared with LSTM. One secondary finding deserves particular attention: the hybrid model performed better for influenza B than for influenza A. The authors note this explicitly, and it is biologically plausible. Influenza B tends to exhibit more regular and less genetically volatile epidemic behaviour than influenza A, which is subject to more frequent antigenic drift and occasional shift and can produce earlier or more erratic season onsets. A forecasting framework that leans on stable seasonal structure, as the SARIMA backbone does, will naturally fare better with a pathogen whose dynamics are themselves more stable. Influenza A’s greater unpredictability leaves more residual noise for any model, hybrid or otherwise, to struggle with, and the smaller margin of improvement for influenza A against the standalone LSTM hints at that ceiling. The practical implications extend beyond the metrics. Local healthcare institutions and disease-control agencies operate under real constraints: vaccine campaigns must be timed, antiviral stockpiles allocated, staff rosters adjusted, and hospital beds and testing capacity planned months in advance. A model that reliably trims forecast error by roughly seven to nine percent, even on monthly case counts from a single hospital, translates into earlier and more accurate warnings of when the seasonal wave will build and peak. The authors position the model as an auxiliary reference rather than a replacement for expert judgement, which is the appropriate framing: hospital-derived positive case counts are influenced by testing practices and care-seeking behaviour, and any forecast built on them inherits those biases. Still, as a complement to national sentinel systems, a locally trained model grounded in the actual case flow of a specific institution offers a granularity that broad regional surveillance cannot. The study also illustrates a broader trend in infectious-disease modelling: the convergence of classical statistical methods and machine learning into hybrid frameworks that play to the strengths of each. Purely statistical models remain interpretable and data-efficient; neural networks capture nonlinearities but demand more data and careful regularisation. Combining them, as this Jiande team has done with a modest six-year dataset, shows that useful gains do not require enormous data volumes or exotic architectures, only a thoughtful division of labour between the two approaches. As climate variability, post-pandemic shifts in respiratory-virus circulation, and evolving vaccination patterns continue to perturb the once-reliable rhythm of influenza seasons, tools that squeeze additional accuracy out of routine surveillance data will only grow in value for the clinicians and public-health officials who must act on their predictions. records.content: 21财经APP 南财号 数字报 越声智投 首页 宏观 公司 金融 证券 全球 观点 汽车 新健康 人文 智库 更多 大湾区 一带一路 文旅 理财 投资通 21视频 直播 品牌活动 首页 粤港澳 正文 @广东街坊:流感疫苗安排上!每年10-11月打最合适 2026年10月10日 16:45 广东药监 流感季一来 家里老人、孩子、慢性病患者 最容易被盯上 接种流感疫苗 是预防流感最经济、最有效的手段 为大家整理了流感和流感疫苗接种知识 广东街坊看过来 流感不是普通感冒 流感由流感病毒感染引起,是急性呼吸道传染病,呈季节性流行。普通感冒可由鼻病毒等多种病原体引起,常在受凉、气候突变、过度疲劳等情况下发生。 症状上,流感表现为咽喉痛、干咳、鼻塞、流涕,还可能伴有高热、寒战、头痛、肌肉关节酸痛、乏力等全身症状。严重时可导致肺炎、心肌损伤、休克等并发症,部分人可发展为重症、危重症甚至死亡。 普通感冒主要是咽痛、流涕、鼻塞、咳嗽等呼吸道症状,较少出现全身症状,或仅有轻微乏力,很少出现严重并发症。 高发季节是什么时候? 广东省流感每年秋季起逐渐进入流行季,冬春季(每年11月至次年3月)是流感等呼吸道传染病高发季节,流行高峰通常出现在12月中下旬至次年1月初。除冬春季高峰外,广东省也存在夏季流行。不同季节、不同年份流行的流感病毒存在差异,同一流行季内也可能出现优势毒株交替。 哪些人更容易中招? 流感病毒易发生变异,人群普遍易感。 60岁及以上老人、5岁以下儿童,以及患有基础性疾病的人群,是流感高风险人群,感染后出现严重并发症的风险较高。 当前在人群中传播流行的,主要是甲型流感病毒H1N1亚型、H3N2亚型,以及乙型流感病毒Victoria系。三者会交替或叠加出现,形成每年的季节性流行。 哪些人建议优先接种? 建议6月龄及以上且没有接种禁忌的人员,每年接种流感疫苗。 优先接种人群 1.60岁及以上老年人、慢性病患者、6月龄-5岁儿童,养老机构、长期护理机构、福利院居住人员等。 这类人群感染流感后,容易发生肺炎等并发症,也可能加重原有基础性疾病。 2.托幼机构和中小学校学生、医务人员等。 这类人群感染风险较高,也建议优先接种。接种疫苗不仅保护自己,也能保护身边感染后容易发展成重症的人。 为什么每年都要打? 流感病毒易变异,当年流行毒株和往年不完全一样,疫苗成分会根据监测情况更新。接种后的保护作用也会随着时间逐渐减弱。 所以,流感疫苗不是“一次接种、长期有效”,而是建议每个流行季按程序接种。同一流行季完成全程接种后,无需重复接种。 接种后通常需要2-4周才能产生具有保护水平的抗体。建议在流行季来临前完成接种。综合广东流感冬春季流行特点,建议每年9-11月完成接种;如果错过这个时间,整个流行季期间任何时候都可以接种。 今年疫苗组分有变化吗? 全球使用的流感疫苗株,每年由世界卫生组织基于全球流感监测数据进行更新推荐。与上一年度相比,本年度三种疫苗组分均有更新。 世界卫生组织推荐的2026—2027年度北半球基于鸡胚生产的三价流感疫苗组分为: A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus 今年为什么只有三价? 过去四价流感疫苗中的第4个组分,主要针对B/Yamagata系病毒。世界卫生组织根据全球流感监测结果认为,自2020年3月以来一直没有发现自然感染的B/Yamagata系流感病毒,因此不必在流感疫苗中继续保留这一组分,并建议各国逐步从四价疫苗转换为三价疫苗。 今年起,全国批准上市的流感疫苗均为三价疫苗,包括裂解疫苗、亚单位疫苗和鼻喷减毒活疫苗等剂型。 所以,从四价变成三价,并不是少打了一种、效果“缩水”了,而是没必要的去掉了,需要的及时更新了。 有高血压、糖尿病等基础病的老人 能打吗? 可以。有慢性病,并不意味着不能接种流感疫苗。相反,老年人和慢性病患者感染流感后,发生重症和并发症的风险更高,国家流感疫苗接种指南也将慢性病患者列为优先推荐接种人群。 关键看现在身体状况是否稳定。如果高血压、糖尿病等基础病控制稳定,没有发热等不适,一般可以接种。如果正处于疾病急性发作期,或出现发热、明显不舒服,建议先暂缓,等身体状况稳定后再接种。 接种前,要把健康情况如实告诉接种医生或工作人员,由专业人员评估是否适合接种。 打完疫苗要注意什么? 接种后应在接种单位留观30分钟,无异常后方可离开。 少数人接种后可能出现接种部位红肿、疼痛或低热等轻微反应,一般1-2天可自行缓解。如出现持续不适,应及时就医,并告知接种单位。 打了流感疫苗, 为什么还可能得流感? 流感病毒易变异,流行株与疫苗株可能不完全匹配;接种后还要2-4周才产生保护抗体;保护效果也会随时间逐渐减弱。 因此,疫苗无法100%预防感染。但疫苗的核心价值在于显著降低重症、住院和死亡风险。即使发生感染,接种过疫苗的人通常症状更轻、病程更短,出现严重并发症以及发展为重症或死亡的风险也更低。 得过流感,还要打吗? 需要。 同一个流感流行季中,可能会有不同病毒型别或亚型共同或交替流行。在广东,通常除了冬春季,还存在夏季流行季,流行型别或亚型也通常不同。不同亚型之间缺乏有效交叉保护,感染过其中一种后,仍可能再感染其他类型。即使曾经得过流感,仍建议在符合接种条件的情况下,接种当前流行季流感疫苗,降低再次感染其他型别或亚型、发生并发症和重症的风险。 如果正处于发热、急性发病或慢性病急性发作期,可待痊愈或病情稳定后再接种。 除了接种疫苗,还要做什么? 1.勤洗手、室内常通风、科学戴口罩、流行季少聚集,可减少感染流感的风险。 2.加强日常锻炼。多参加户外活动,合理搭配膳食,提高自身免疫力。 3.做好自我监测,若出现发热、咳嗽、咽痛、肌肉酸痛等流感样症状,请及时就医。 流感疫苗每年都要打。2026-2027流行季,建议10-11月完成接种;错过这个时间,整个流行季期间任何时候都可以接种。 早打早保护 转给家人,流感疫苗安排起来~ 素材来源:“广东疾控”公众号 编辑整理:广东药监 返回21经济网首页 >> 分享到: × 分享到微信朋友圈 打开微信,点击底部的“发现”, 使用“扫一扫”即可将网页分享至朋友圈。 相关新闻 热文排行 1 “向佐喝蛋白粉把肾喝成70岁”冲上热搜:如何补蛋白、护肾脏? By Olivia Maule Edited by Nicoletta Lanese, Laura Mondragón Published 9 October 2026 In News Flu cases are rising unusually early in several Western states this fall. (Image credit: KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY via Getty Images) Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Flu season is off to an early start in some parts of the U.S., data shows. In a typical year, U.S. flu activity starts building in late fall — typically in October or November — and peaks between December and February. This year, flu activity is currently low but rising nationwide: During the week ending Sept. 26, 3.4% of respiratory samples tested by clinical labs were positive for flu, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data. That's about seven times the rate that was seen at the same point last year. About 0.5% of samples tested positive during the week ending Sept. 27, 2025. Latest Videos FromLive Science Watch full video here: "This particular year, it appears to be starting early — like right now," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health in Tennessee, told Live Science. Patients at clinics in his area are already testing positive for flu, he said. The early uptick in flu is mostly unfolding in Western states, including Washington, California and Arizona. In Washington, for example, the share of emergency department visits diagnosed as flu climbed from 0.25% in the week ending Aug. 29 to 1.34% in the week ending Oct. 3, according to CDC emergency department data. That's a more than fivefold increase over six weeks. Where the flu took off first isn't a warning sign in itself, Schaffner noted. "There's nothing unusual about flu starting in the West Coast and moving east," he said. Recent seasons have more often begun in the Southeast or Midwest, he noted, but "it can start almost anywhere." Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Leading with H1N1 Nowadays, seasonal flu is caused by three subtypes of flu viruses: two subtypes of influenza A, called H1N1 and H3N2, and the Victoria lineage of influenza B. (A second subtype of influenza B used to circulate but is now thought to be extinct.) Last season, a fast-spreading version of H3N2 known as subclade K dominated. The CDC classified the 2025-2026 season as highly severe for children, as at least 195 children died of flu-related causes. Schaffner likens influenza A and B to siblings. "They're very related, but they each have their own individual characteristics," he said. Influenza A strains usually cause the biggest outbreaks early in the season, while influenza B strains "kind of smolder along" and account for most cases toward the end, he noted. This year, H1N1 has taken the initial lead. Of the influenza A samples that public health labs subtyped during the week ending Sept. 26, 96% were identified as H1N1, according to CDC data. That doesn't mean H1N1 will continue to dominate throughout the season; it just gives a snapshot of what's happening now. The dominant strain matters because flu is "a moving target," said Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. The virus constantly mutates — especially hemagglutinin, the protein on the virus's surface that it uses to latch onto human cells. Hemagglutinin is the main target of flu vaccines. An early start to the season doesn't guarantee it'll be a severe one, either. In its 2026-2027 season outlook, the CDC projected that this season will likely be moderate, although it has only low-to-moderate confidence in that forecast. Everyone ages 6 months and older is recommended to get a flu shot, and older adults have several options, including high-dose, adjuvanted and mRNA vaccines. (Image credit: andreswd via Getty Images) When to get vaccinated Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu vaccine. Influenza is especially dangerous for children under 5, adults 65 and older, people with chronic health conditions and pregnant people, as these groups are more prone to severe infections. Serious cases of flu can lead to complications such as pneumonia, sepsis, and brain or heart inflammation, and in some cases, they can be deadly. Tens of thousands of people die of flu each season in the U.S. For flu vaccination, timing matters. The CDC generally doesn't recommend vaccination in July or August for most adults, because the shot's protection can wane over the course of a season. But with flu arriving early, "October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, and even more so right now," Schaffner said. When circulating strains' features differ from those captured in the vaccine, "that usually predicts a more difficult season," Offit said. That said, it's too early to know if this year's flu shots are a good match for the circulating flu viruses. Protection begins building right after you get the shot, but it takes up to about two weeks to reach full strength. How much protection a flu vaccine offers varies by season, depending partly on how well its formulation matches the strains that circulate. Offit said that protection against symptomatic illness varies by age group and that the vaccines are "a little more effective" at preventing more severe illness. In terms of flu cases that prompt people to seek medical care, the shot has been 29% to 56% effective over the past decade, the CDC estimates. While the vaccines are less reliable at preventing mild cases of flu, Schaffner said, they work best at "keeping you out of the hospital, keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery." The CDC's 2026-2027 guidance keeps its recommendation of an annual flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older, with high-dose and adjuvanted shots preferred for adults 65 and older. (Adjuvanted shots contain an extra ingredient to help rev up the immune system.) There's also a new option: In August, the Food and Drug Administration approved mFlusiva, the first mRNA flu vaccine, for adults 50 and older. Flu Season Started Early in Parts of the U.S., and Experts Say You Should Consider Getting the Seasonal Jab ASAP. Here’s What to Know The season usually starts in October or November. But some western states, including California, Washington, Alaska and Hawaii, began seeing a rise in flu cases as early as August Sara Hashemi | Daily Correspondent October 8, 2026 Share Copy linkEmailSMSFacebookXRedditLinkedInBlueskyPrint Add as preferred source An early start to the season doesn't necessarily mean it'll be a more severe one than usual, according to health professionals. Iparraguirre Recio via Getty Images Every year, autumn brings gorgeous foliage, crisp air, shorter days—and a slew of respiratory illnesses. Flu season usually starts in October or November, but infection data suggests it has kicked off early in parts of the Northern Hemisphere. Report Ad Flu rates began rising in August or September in many western states, including California, Washington, Alaska and Hawaii. That’s unusual because the respiratory illness typically starts in the Southeast and spreads toward the West Coast. Infection rates have also been unusually early in places like Japan and the United Kingdom. We’re “looking at an early flu season this year,” said James Watt, deputy director of infectious diseases at the California Department of Public Health, at a briefing on October 6, reports Catherine Ho at the San Francisco Chronicle. This early rise is concerning because people haven’t started getting their vaccines yet, says Danielle Zerr, an infectious-diseases specialist at Seattle Children’s, to Lena H. Sun at the Washington Post. “The way flu is circulating now, you wanted that vaccine in you two weeks ago, if not even a little before that.” Here’s what you need to know about this year’s early flu season. What is the flu? The flu is caused by an infection with an influenza virus. There are two subtypes of Influenza A—H3N2 and H1N1—and one type of Influenza B, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The severity of each season depends on which version of the virus is spreading. H3N2 influenza strains are linked to more severe flu seasons and more hospitalizations. This year, the other one, H1N1, is dominating. Flu spreads via droplets spewed when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks. Symptoms generally appear one to four days after infection. Signs of illness can include fever or feverish chills, cough, sore throat, runny nose, muscle aches and fatigue. A sick individual is most contagious during their first three days of symptoms. Quick fact: Annual toll Since 2010, the flu has resulted in between 120,000 and 710,000 hospitalizations and has contributed to between 6,300 and 52,000 deaths each year in the U.S., according to estimates by the CDC. Why is this year’s flu season early? Experts don’t know for sure, but one possibility is that a new variant of H1N1 evolved a mutation that is better at evading some people’s immune systems. “That’s our best argument for what’s going on right now in terms of this early flu season,” says Alex Greninger, a virologist at the University of Washington, to Rob Stein at NPR. Another reason might be that because H3N2 dominated last year’s flu season, people have less recent immunity against the version that’s currently running rampant, Helen Chu, an infectious-diseases specialist at the University of Washington, tells the Washington Post. It’s still too soon to tell what this year’s season will look like. Looking at the Southern Hemisphere can offer clues, since our seasons are flipped, writes Katelyn Jetelina for Your Local Epidemiologist. “Flu season was severe in many places this summer,” she explains, with Argentina recording its highest number of flu-like illness cases in a decade. That doesn’t necessarily mean things will look the same in the Northern Hemisphere, but it’s something epidemiologists are keeping an eye on. What’s more, “an early start doesn’t necessarily mean a more severe season,” says James Hay, an epidemiologist at the University of Oxford in England, to Nature’s Mariana Lenharo. How can I protect myself? Flu vaccines for 2026-27 are already available, and the best thing you can do is get your shot as early as possible—even if you got one last year. The vaccine is adjusted every year to target the strains that researchers predict will be circulating that season. While it’s hard for them to get it exactly right, vaccines still offer an important level of protection that can reduce the severity of the illness. “This is one of those seasons where the key message is to go get vaccinated now,” Greninger tells Nature. However, this flu season might be different. Traditionally, cases start to ramp up in October or November, but according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), an uptick in infections has already begun in early September 2026 compared with the same week in 2025. Although flu activity is generally still very low, the flu season would typically begin in the southern states and not in the West. Its error-prone RNA polymerase introduces mutations with every replication cycle, allowing the virus to gradually reshape the very surfaces that human antibodies recognize. A new whole-genome sequencing study from Iran, published in Virology Journal, has now provided one of the most detailed national pictures yet of how this virus evolved across two consecutive influenza seasons, from 2023 to 2025, and what that evolution means for vaccine performance. The work, led by researchers at Tehran University of Medical Sciences in collaboration with the Iran National Influenza Center, sequenced thirty complete viral genomes collected during the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 seasons, using Oxford Nanopore Technology to read all eight genomic segments of each isolate. The choice of platform matters. Whole-genome sequencing with nanopore devices allows laboratories to generate complete viral genomes rapidly and at relatively low cost, which is essential for surveillance programs that need to keep pace with a virus that evolves on a timescale of months. Rather than focusing solely on the hemagglutinin gene, the conventional workhorse of influenza phylogenetics, the Iranian team examined the entire genome, including the internal proteins that govern replication efficiency, host immune modulation, and antiviral susceptibility. This comprehensive approach is increasingly recognized as essential because changes outside the surface glycoproteins can influence viral fitness and virulence in ways that hemagglutinin-focused studies miss entirely. The central finding concerns genetic distance from the vaccine strain. Viruses circulating during the 2024–2025 season showed slightly lower nucleotide similarity to the vaccine component, at 98.78 percent, than those from the 2023–2024 season, which stood at 99.13 percent. While a difference of roughly a third of a percentage point may appear trivial, in influenza virology such incremental drift is precisely what accumulates into antigenic change over successive seasons. The result confirms that the Iranian viral population was not static between the two seasons but continued to diverge slowly from the A/Wisconsin/67/2022 vaccine strain, mirroring the global pattern of antigenic drift that the World Health Organization monitors when it convenes its twice-yearly vaccine composition meetings. Discover more Get Cold Relief Order DNA Kits vaccine Find Vaccines To translate raw sequence divergence into immunological terms, the researchers turned their attention to the epitope landscape of the hemagglutinin protein. Epitopes are the discrete regions of viral surface proteins that antibodies actually bind, and mutations concentrated within these regions are far more consequential for immune escape than changes elsewhere in the protein. The analysis revealed that epitope A, one of the five major antigenic sites on the globular head of hemagglutinin, was the most variable region during both seasons. This is consistent with decades of influenza research showing that epitope A sits at the immunodominant tip of the molecule, where antibody pressure is strongest and where substitutions are most readily tolerated structurally. Using a computational method that estimates vaccine efficacy from the density of substitutions within epitope regions, the team calculated that vaccine protection against the dominant epitope ranged from 38.1 percent to 50.5 percent across the 2023–2025 period. These figures, while moderate, fall within the range typically observed for inactivated influenza vaccines in well-matched seasons, where real-world effectiveness against laboratory-confirmed infection often hovers between 40 and 60 percent. The authors interpret these estimates as acceptable and consistent with the WHO decision to retain A/Wisconsin/67/2022 as the H1N1 component of the 2025–2026 seasonal vaccine. In other words, despite measurable drift, the circulating Iranian viruses had not yet escaped the reach of vaccine-induced immunity. Beyond the surface glycoproteins, the study documented several substitutions in the internal proteins of the viral genome, a dimension of influenza evolution that receives far less attention in routine surveillance. Among these, the I123V substitution in the non-structural protein NS1 was detected in both the vaccine strain and the analyzed Iranian isolates. NS1 is a multifunctional virulence factor that antagonizes the host interferon response, and substitutions in this protein can modulate how effectively the virus suppresses innate immunity. The presence of the same substitution in both vaccine and circulating strains suggests it is a shared, likely stable feature of the clade rather than a marker of emerging virulence specific to the Iranian isolates. Antiviral susceptibility is the other critical surveillance question, and here the news was largely reassuring. Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir remain the mainstay of influenza antiviral therapy, and resistance mutations in the neuraminidase gene can rapidly undermine treatment, as occurred historically with seasonal H1N1 strains that acquired the H275Y substitution. The Iranian viruses remained largely susceptible to neuraminidase inhibitors throughout the study period, although one strain carried the S247N substitution, a change that has been associated with reduced inhibition in some influenza A viruses and therefore warrants continued monitoring. A single resistant-adjacent variant among thirty genomes does not signal a treatment crisis, but it illustrates exactly the kind of signal that whole-genome surveillance is designed to catch early. Discover more Vaccine vaccines Check Symptoms Study Biology genomes Phylogenetic analysis placed 90 percent of the Iranian strains within clade 6B.1 A.5a.2a, the same subclade that dominated globally during the 2023–2025 seasons. This clustering demonstrates that Iran’s H1N1 population was fully integrated into the worldwide viral lineage structure, with no evidence of a locally divergent or geographically isolated evolutionary trajectory. The researchers also compared the topologies of phylogenetic trees built from different genomic segments, a standard approach for detecting reassortment, the process by which co-infecting viruses exchange entire segments and can generate strains with novel combinations of surface and internal genes. Despite minor topological differences among the trees, no reassortment was detected, indicating that the Iranian viruses evolved through gradual point mutation rather than segment exchange. The broader significance of the study lies less in any single mutation than in the demonstration of what sustained national sequencing capacity can deliver. Iran sits at a crossroads of human migration and viral traffic, and genomic data from the region fill an important gap in the global influenza surveillance network, which has historically been concentrated in North America, Europe, and East Asia. By showing that circulating strains remained closely matched to the vaccine, that epitope-level drift was measurable but not yet consequential, and that antiviral susceptibility was preserved, the study provides exactly the kind of evidence that informs vaccine strain selection committees and public health planners. The authors emphasize that continued national surveillance within global frameworks is essential for monitoring antigenic change, assessing pandemic risk, guiding vaccine updates, and detecting antiviral resistance before it becomes widespread. For the coming seasons, the message is one of cautious continuity rather than alarm. The H1N1 viruses circulating in Iran between 2023 and 2025 drifted measurably, concentrated their changes in the most immunologically visible regions of hemagglutinin, and edged slightly further from the vaccine strain with each season, yet they remained recognizably the same clade 6B.1 A.5a.2a viruses that the current vaccine was designed to counter. The estimated epitope-based vaccine efficacy of roughly 38 to 50 percent suggests meaningful, if imperfect, protection, in line with expectations for a well-matched seasonal vaccine. As sequencing technology becomes cheaper and faster, studies of this kind are likely to become the norm rather than the exception, offering public health authorities a near-real-time view of viral evolution and a firmer scientific footing for the annual decisions that determine how well the world’s influenza vaccines match the viruses they must fight.
